skill.name: Emotive words: spot them and say it neutrally
skill.why: Emotive words push your feelings. Spotting them lets you think for yourself.
skill.how: Find words loaded with feeling. Swap each for a calm word that means the same.

steps.say: The council closed our skate park. Zed is cross!

show.nudge: 'Council' just names who did it. Which word makes them sound mean?
'Skate park' just names the place. Which word makes you feel cross?

steps.ask: Tap the word picked to make you feel angry.
steps.win: Yes! Snatched pushes your feelings. A word like that is emotive.

steps.say: Say it calmly. Keep what happened. Drop the push.
steps.ask: Which says Zed's sentence without the push?

options.reason: Snatched is still there, and 'sadly' adds more feeling.

encounters.frame: Two writers described the same dingo pups. The Puffentie is sorting their sentences, one word at a time.
encounters.text: Last week, rangers found two dingo pups alone near a dry creek bed, about ten kilometres from Bluster Rock. Their mother had not been seen for several days. The pups were thin and had not eaten for days. They were taken to the Red Dust Dingo Rescue, where volunteers are feeding them every four hours. The pups are about six weeks old and weigh just over a kilogram each. The ranger's report noted that the creek had been dry for three months. Volunteers have named the pups Red and Dusty. Two people wrote about the pups: a ranger, for the council, and the Vantamart, for an ad selling photos with the pups. Mo has mixed up their sentences. The rescue centre says the pups are healthy and putting on weight. They will stay at the centre until they are old enough to move to a wildlife sanctuary. Wren has offered to help with the night feeds.

encounters.frame: The Bugle is reporting on Maxx's rocket launch, using Maxx's own words. The editor is not happy.
encounters.text: On Tuesday morning, Maxx Vantablack's Gold Rocket launched from a paddock behind the Vantamart. The launch had been delayed twice because of strong winds. A crowd of about 2,000 people watched from the beach, and many more watched live on Maxx's channel. Tickets to watch from the beach cost $50, and about half the crowd wore gold sunglasses handed out by Maxx's Goldies. The rocket rose to a height of 80 kilometres before its parachutes opened and it drifted back down to the red sand. Maxx himself was not on board, although he wore a gold space suit for the cameras. The rocket is now being cleaned and checked, and Maxx says it will fly again next month. The Bugle's new reporter wrote the story using words from Maxx's own press release, including this sentence: 'Maxx's magnificent rocket soared triumphantly 80 kilometres into the sky.' The editor has asked for a neutral version. Readers, she says, can decide for themselves whether it was magnificent.

encounters.frame: A customer's complaint about a Chore-Bot has reached the Bugle. The Puffentie wants a calm version.
encounters.text: Dear Editor, I bought a Chore-Bot from Slick Vinnie's stall at the Bluster Rock market last Saturday. Vinnie promised it would fold washing, wipe benches and feed the cat. Vinnie told me the Chore-Bot was the 'deal of the century' and that I would never fold washing again. I paid $80 for it. On Sunday, I asked it to fold my son's school shirt. Instead of folding it, that useless heap of junk mauled my son's school shirt! It tore a long hole down the back, and then it tried to fold the cat. The cat is fine, but it now hides whenever it hears a beep. He was right about one thing: I haven't folded any washing since, because I've been too busy sewing. When I took the robot back to the market, Vinnie said the shirt must have been 'faulty'. I would like other readers to know what happened before they spend $80. Yours faithfully, Dot Kelly, Saltbush Road
encounters.prompt: Build a neutral sentence that says what the Chore-Bot did to the shirt. Keep the facts in the letter.
encounters.success: 'Tore' is calm and true. 'Mauled' pushed anger, and 'creased' or 'folded' would hide the long hole.

accept: The Chore-Bot tore my son's school shirt.
body.reason: Check the letter. The robot left a long hole. Pick the calm word that still says so.

encounters.frame: Ada Pennick's letter is going to the council, but the clerk says it needs to be calmer. The Puffentie agrees.
encounters.text: Dear Councillors, I am writing on behalf of the Bluster Bay Turtle Volunteers to ask you to cancel the licence that allows jet ski hire in the bay. For decades, the northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles. Every summer, our volunteers count the nests, fence them off and watch the hatchlings scramble down to the water by moonlight. Since the hire shop opened in October, rangers have found fourteen injured turtles in the bay, most of them with cuts that match the shape of a propeller. My first draft of this letter included the following sentence: 'Reckless thrill-seekers on roaring jet skis have mown down fourteen defenceless turtles in our once-peaceful bay.' The council clerk has kindly pointed out that councillors are more likely to listen to the facts if they are not wrapped in so much feeling, and that the rangers' figures are powerful enough on their own. I have therefore agreed to rewrite it. I would be grateful if you could read the rangers' report before the vote on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer

encounters.prompt: The report says Vinnie 'shamelessly' doubled his price. What does that one word do to readers?
encounters.success: 'Shamelessly' judges Vinnie for you. A neutral report says he doubled his price and lets readers decide.

options.text: It pushes readers to think badly of Vinnie before they decide for themselves.
It tells readers exactly how much Vinnie has raised the price of his tour.
options.reason: 'Doubled' and '$5 to $10' tell you that. This word adds a judgement.

options.text: It shows readers that Vinnie felt ashamed about raising the price of his tour.
options.reason: Shameless means without shame. The word blames Vinnie. It doesn't say he felt bad.

options.text: It gives readers a fact they could check against Vinnie's ticket sales.
options.reason: You can count tickets, but you can't count shame. This word is a judgement.

encounters.text: MYSTERY LIGHTS: COUNCIL TO INVESTIGATE. For the past two weeks, green lights have been seen above the old mine at the back of Bluster Rock, usually between 11 pm and midnight. The lights were first reported by a truck driver, who saw them while driving past the rock on his way to Saltbush Creek. A security camera at the service station recorded the lights on three separate nights, and several residents of Dune Street have reported a low humming noise coming from the mine after dark. The council has now asked a team of scientists to examine the site. Ghost tour guide Slick Vinnie has shamelessly doubled the price of his midnight tour, from $5 to $10, and says that ticket sales have tripled since the lights first appeared. One scientist, Dr Esther Okafor, has suggested that the lights may come from a glowing fungus that grows on old mine timbers. The scientists are expected to visit the mine next Tuesday and will take samples from the tunnels. Their findings will be shared at a public meeting in the town hall. The mine has been closed since 1923, and the council has asked the public to stay away from the entrance until the scientists have finished their work. The Soggy Biscuit crew has offered to help.

encounters.frame: Two letters about the music festival are in today's Bugle. The Puffentie is sorting their phrases, and puffing furiously.
encounters.text: The council's plan to bring back the Bluster Rock Music Festival has divided the town, and this week the Bugle received two very different letters about it. The first came from Jojo Reyes, the lead singer of Red Dust Static, who wants the festival to return next autumn. She called it 'a joyous celebration' full of 'crowds of happy music lovers', and reminded readers that the 2019 festival attracted 6,000 visitors. Her letter also said the festival would bring money to local shops, and she asked readers to support it at the council meeting. The second came from Pat Grumbleton of Dune Street, who described the old festival as 'a deafening, sleepless nightmare' and complained about 'rowdy mobs' trampling his front garden. Pat said he had lived on Dune Street for forty years, and he asked the council to think of residents who need their sleep. The Bugle has decided to print both letters in full on page five. Both letters included some neutral details: the festival was held every autumn until 2019, it had loud music until 11 pm, and it used a stage built on a flatbed truck. The council will vote on the plan at its meeting on 3 March, and residents are welcome to attend.
encounters.prompt: Put each phrase from the letters in the right box.
encounters.success: Emotive words push you one way or the other. A number used to win you over can still be neutral.

emotive: makes you dread the festival

items.reason: 'Joyous' is picked to make you feel happy about the festival.
'Happy music lovers' paints the crowd warmly, so you want them back.
'Nightmare' wants you to dread the festival. It's emotive.
'Mobs' makes visitors sound dangerous, and 'rowdy' adds a push against them.
Jojo uses this number to win you over, but the words are plain. You could check it.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing up his mould experiment for the science fair judges. Wren says one word is too dramatic.
encounters.text: For his science fair project, Gus left five foods in sealed jars for fourteen days. The jars sat on the windowsill of the Soggy Biscuit's galley. The foods were white bread, an orange, cheese, a boiled potato and one of Mo's fish-finger custards. He photographed each jar at the same time every morning and measured how much of the surface was covered in mould. The bread grew mould first, on day three, and the orange was completely covered by day ten. Wren checked the jars each morning to make sure the lids were still tight. The cheese grew the least mould of the real foods, and Mo's custard grew none at all, which worried everyone. On day fourteen, Gus opened the jars to take samples, and a smell spread through the galley that was so strong Tully moved her hammock onto the deck. Mo said it reminded him of his cousin's football boots. The science fair judges have asked for reports that are calm and exact, because, as the head judge puts it, 'good science describes, it doesn't dramatise'. Gus has written most of his report in that style, but one word in his description of day fourteen still gives away how he felt.
encounters.prompt: Tap the emotive word in Gus's report. Then choose the calm word that keeps all the facts.
encounters.success: 'Strong' keeps how powerful the smell was. 'Unusual' is calm too, but it drops what made Tully move.

parts.reason: 'Fourteen' just tells you which day. You could check Gus's notes.
'Mouldy' sounds gross, but Gus measured the mould. It's an exact fact, not a push.
'Filled' says how far the smell spread. Mo and Tully would agree, so it's neutral.

encounters.frame: Maxx is reading out a news story about Bluster Rock Primary on his stream. The Puffentie can barely keep still.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! Big news today from Bluster Rock Primary. The school has announced that its brass bell, which has rung at the start of every lunch for sixty years, will be replaced next term by a robot that sings. The robot is about the size of a toaster, and it will sit on the staffroom roof. Principal Okafor says it can sing twelve different songs, including one about the canteen. Some students have started a petition to keep the bell, and so far it has forty names on it. The bell itself will be polished and put in a glass case in the school foyer. Of course, my channel has its own take on the story. My writers came up with this headline: 'Heartless principal ruthlessly dumps beloved bell for screeching tin-can robot.' Is it a bit much? Maybe. But that's Maxx-imum content! Some of you, especially the haters, have asked whether I would ever swap my alarm clock for a singing robot. Never, Vantafam. Nobody sings like me. The Bugle wants the story too. Its two subeditors each rewrote my headline. Version A: 'Principal replaces school bell with singing robot.' Version B: 'Principal swaps much-loved bell for singing robot.' Smash that heart button like it owes you money! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: The Bugle wants a neutral headline. Which version should it print, and why?
encounters.success: A just tells the news. B quietly adds 'much-loved', which pushes readers to side with the bell.

options.text: A, because it reports the change and leaves the feelings to readers.
B, because forty names on a petition prove the bell is much-loved.
options.reason: Forty names is a fact, but B's describing word still pushes you to feel sad.

options.text: B, because 'swaps' is a calmer word than 'replaces'.
options.reason: Both of those words are calm. The push in B is hiding somewhere else.

options.text: Either one, because neither keeps Maxx's loaded words 'heartless' or 'screeching'.
options.reason: B drops Maxx's words, but it adds a new push of its own.

encounters.frame: Maxx is boasting about his painting again. The Bugle wants one plain sentence for its news page.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! I have the most incredible news. Last night, at the Bluster Rock Art Auction, my painting 'Gold on Gold' was sold to a mystery collector from overseas. The painting is two metres wide and covered in real gold leaf. The buyer has not been named, but they have 'excellent taste, obviously'. The auction raised $95,000 in total, from forty-two paintings. Let me say that again, louder, for the haters at the back: my genius, jaw-dropping painting sold for a mind-blowing $40,000! That is more than any painting has ever sold for at the Bluster Rock auction, and it's the second year in a row that I've broken the record. The auctioneer has even confirmed it, which I think is very generous of her. I painted it in under ten minutes, using a brush made from my own hair, which I think we can all agree is the most important hair in the world. As always, every cent goes to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund. The Bugle wants to report the sale on its news page tomorrow, but its editor has asked for one plain sentence that tells readers the facts without any of my sparkle. Boring! Two Xs, because one X is for losers! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: Build a calm sentence about the sale that still shows how big the price was. Start with 'Maxx's'.
encounters.success: 'A record' is calm and checkable: no painting at the auction ever sold for more. It keeps the price's size.

accept: Maxx's painting sold for a record $40,000.
body.reason: Check each describing tile. 'Modest' shrinks the price, and 'genius' or 'mind-blowing' push. One tile is calm and true.
